items.title: Three More Wrong Motives: Competitive Pride, Grooming, and Vanity

items.zh: 謂如有一樂受欲者，為受諸欲食於所食。彼作是思：我今宜應多食所食、飽食所食，隨力隨能食噉肥膩，增房補益，色香味具精妙飲食。過今夜分至於明日，於角武事當有力能。所謂按摩、拍毱、托石、跳躑、蹴蹋、攘臂、扼腕、揮戈、擊劍、伏弩、控弦、投輪、擲索，依如是等諸角武事，當得勇健，膚體充實，長夜無病，久時少壯，不速衰老，壽命長遠，能多噉食，數數食已能正消化，除諸疾患。如是為於無病憍逸、少壯憍逸、長壽憍逸而食所食。既角武已，復作是思：我應沐浴。便以種種清淨香水沐浴其身；沐浴身已，梳理其髮；梳理髮已，種種妙香用塗其身；既塗身已，復以種種上妙衣服、種種花鬘、種種嚴具莊飾其身。此中沐浴、理髮、塗香，名為飾好；既飾好已，復以種種上妙衣服、花鬘、嚴具莊飾其身，名為端嚴。
items.en: It is like one who delights in sensual pleasure, eating for the sake of experiencing those pleasures. Such a person thinks: "I should now eat much, eat until full, eating rich and fatty foods to the limit of my strength and capacity, food that boosts sexual vigour and nourishes the body, excellent food complete in colour, aroma, and taste. When this night passes into tomorrow, I shall have the strength for feats of contest." …Through such feats of contest, one gains vigour and strength, a firm and full physique, freedom from illness over a long span, lasting youthfulness, no premature ageing, a long lifespan, the capacity to eat abundantly, and food that digests properly each time, free of any ailment. This is eating for the sake of pride in freedom from illness, pride in lasting youth, and pride in longevity. …Having competed, one further thinks: "I should bathe." One then bathes the body with various kinds of pure, fragrant water; having bathed, one combs and arranges the hair; having done so, one applies various fine fragrances to the body; and, having done so, one further adorns the body with various fine garments, garlands, and ornaments. Bathing, combing the hair, and applying fragrance are called grooming; adorning the body afterwards with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments is called elegance.

items.zh: 如是總名為飾好故、為端嚴故食於所食。

items.title: Section: The Four Wrong Motives Close — Eating Only to Sustain the Body

items.zh: 彼既如是憍逸、飾好、身端嚴已，於日中分或日後分，臨欲食時，飢渴並至。於諸飲食極生悕欲、極欣、極樂，不見過患，不知出離，隨得隨食。復為數數倡蕩、憍逸、飾好、端嚴，多食多飲，令身充悅。諸有多聞聖弟子眾，以思擇力，深見過患，善知出離，而食所食；非如前說諸受欲者食於所食。唯作是念：我今習近所不應習、所應斷食，為欲永斷如是食故。云何名為為身安住食於所食？謂飲食已壽命得存，非不飲食壽命存故，名身安住。我今受此所有飲食，壽命得存，當不夭沒；由是因緣，身得安住，能修正行，永斷諸食。
items.en: Having thus indulged in pride, grooming, and elegance, when midday or late afternoon arrives and the time to eat draws near, hunger and thirst both set in. One then feels intense craving for food, intense delight in obtaining it, intense pleasure in eating it — seeing no fault in any of this, knowing nothing of being free of it, eating whatever is obtained the moment it is obtained. …The many learned noble disciples, however, through the power of discernment, see these faults deeply, know well how to be free of them, and eat accordingly — not as those driven by desire eat. They think only this: "I now resort to what ought not to be resorted to — food, which ought to be abandoned — precisely in order to be permanently free of such food." …What is called eating for the sake of the body's sustained existence? It is that, having eaten, life is preserved — whereas without eating, life could not be preserved; this is called the body's sustained existence. I now receive this food so that my life may be preserved and not cut short prematurely; because of this, the body remains sustained, able to cultivate correct practice, and, in time, to be permanently free of the need for any of these forms of food at all.

items.zh: 云何名為為暫支持食於所食？

items.title: Eating for Temporary Support: Nourishment That Helps Versus Nourishment That Harms

items.zh: 謂略說有二種存養。一、有艱難存養，二、無艱難存養。云何名為有艱難存養？謂受如是所有飲食，數增飢羸，困苦重病。或以非法追求飲食，非以正法。得已，染愛、耽嗜、饕餮、迷悶、堅執、湎著受用。或有食已，令身沈重，無所堪能，不任修斷。或有食已，令心遲鈍，不速得定；或有食已，令入出息來往艱難；或有食已，令心數為惛沈睡眠之所纏擾。如是名為有艱難存養。
items.en: In brief, there are two kinds of nourishment: nourishment that is difficult, and nourishment that is not difficult. …It is that, receiving such food, one grows repeatedly weaker and hungrier, afflicted with distress and grave illness. …Or, food sought through improper rather than proper means. …Once obtained, it is received with attachment, craving, gluttony, confusion, rigid grasping, and complete absorption. …Or, having eaten, the body becomes heavy, incapable, unfit for cultivation; or, having eaten, the mind grows dull, unable to quickly attain concentration; or, having eaten, the in-breath and out-breath become laboured; or, having eaten, the mind is repeatedly entangled by dullness and drowsiness. This is called nourishment that is difficult.

items.zh: 云何名為無艱難存養？謂受如是所有飲食，令無飢羸，無有困苦及以重病。或以正法追求飲食，不以非法。既獲得已，不染、不愛，亦不耽嗜、饕餮、迷悶、堅執、湎著而受用之。

blocks.text: The remaining wrong motives, then the right purpose: eating only to sustain the body, and the difference between nourishment that helps and nourishment that harms.

Eating for "pride in freedom from illness, pride in lasting youth, pride in longevity". Master Cháng Bǎi gives the example of athletes eating to build strength for competition. "Bathing, combing the hair, applying fragrance" is grooming; "adorning the body with fine garments and ornaments" is elegance.

subs.head: Eating only to sustain the body

blocks.text: Ordinary people "see no fault in any of this, know nothing of being free of it, and eat whatever is obtained the moment it is obtained". Master Cháng Bǎi: intense craving before obtaining food, intense delight when it comes, intense pleasure in eating. The disciple eats to preserve life, and also wishes to be free of this food eventually. Venerable Miào Jìng: beings of the higher realms take the joy of meditation and the delight of Dharma as food.

Nourishment that is **difficult** (harmful) and **not difficult**. Harmful nourishment is obtained improperly: comparing donors' gifts, seeking gain with gain. Venerable Miào Jìng: a Buddhist who breaks the law and the precepts to get food is pursuing it improperly. It is consumed with "attachment, craving, gluttony", and afterwards "the breath becomes laboured, the body heavy, the mind dull or drowsy". Master Cháng Bǎi: some foods, such as heavy, rich ones, bring drowsiness.

quiz.q: Eating for feats of contest is for which three kinds of pride?
options: pride in freedom from illness, in youth, and in longevity
quiz.why: "This is eating for the sake of pride in freedom from illness, pride in lasting youth, and pride in longevity." Master Cháng Bǎi gives the example of athletes, who are soon beaten by younger rivals and so must stay young.

quiz.q: How does the text distinguish grooming from elegance, and what does Master Cháng Bǎi add about grooming?
options: grooming is dressing; elegance is bathing
bathing, combing, and fragrance are grooming; then garments, garlands, and ornaments are elegance; Cháng Bǎi adds that grooming works on the body itself, including shaving the head
grooming is mental; elegance is physical
quiz.why: "Bathing, combing the hair, and applying fragrance are called grooming; adorning the body afterwards with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments is called elegance." Master Cháng Bǎi: grooming beautifies the body itself — bathing, haircutting, shaving the head, applying scent.

quiz.q: After pride and grooming, when hunger and thirst arrive, how does the one driven by desire eat?
options: with intense craving, delight, and pleasure, seeing no fault, knowing no escape, eating whatever comes the moment it comes
offering to the Three Jewels first
quiz.why: "Seeing no fault in any of this, knowing nothing of being free of it, eating whatever is obtained the moment it is obtained." Master Cháng Bǎi: they do not know to seek release because they do not even know there is such a thing as leaving the three realms.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi assign craving, delight, and pleasure to different moments?
options: craving is before obtaining food; delight is after obtaining it but before eating
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: intense craving is before the food is obtained, longing to eat; intense delight is when it has been obtained but not yet eaten. Intense pleasure is in the eating.

quiz.q: What does the treatise call eating for the body's sustained existence?
options: having eaten, life is preserved; without eating it could not be, so it is called the body's sustained existence
quiz.why: "It is that, having eaten, life is preserved — whereas without eating, life could not be preserved." Venerable Miào Jìng: once the noble path is accomplished one need never eat again — this is "accepting food in order to accomplish the path."

quiz.q: What example of "seeking gain with gain" does Master Cháng Bǎi give as improper pursuit?
options: comparing in front of devotees whose offerings are bigger or better
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: comparing, before the faithful, who gave more or less, better or worse — these are forms of seeking gain with gain, all improper ways of pursuing food.

quiz.q: What can difficult nourishment do after eating, and what food does Master Cháng Bǎi give as an example?
options: make breathing laboured — for example, rice cakes
quiz.why: The text: after some food, in-breath and out-breath become laboured — and some makes the body heavy, the mind dull, or drowsy. Master Cháng Bǎi: some foods, such as rice cakes, make breathing difficult.
